unicode.value: The Language of Anatomy - Foundations of Kinesiology

Introduction to the Anatomical Position

To accurately and consistently describe the human body and its vast range of movements, professionals in health and exercise science need a universal frame of reference. This ensures that a description of a body part's location or a specific movement means the same thing to everyone, regardless of the individual's actual posture at the moment. This fundamental standard, which acts as the starting point for all anatomical descriptions, is known as the Anatomical Position.

Anatomical Position Defined

The Anatomical Position is the universally accepted starting reference point used to specify the locations of body parts relative to one another. Every directional term and description of movement assumes the body begins in this specific stance.

Key Characteristics

  • Standing erect
  • Face forward
  • Arms at the sides
  • Palms facing forward
  • Thumbs facing outward
  • Legs straight
  • Heels & feet together and parallel

This precise position is the foundation upon which all directional terms, which we will explore next, are based.

Directional Terms

Directional terms are like a compass for the human body. They allow professionals to communicate the location of one body part in relation to another with absolute precision. These terms, which often come in opposing pairs, are always used with the assumption that the body is in the anatomical position. This system provides a clear and unambiguous language for describing human anatomy.

Term

Directional Terms

Superior / Inferior

Superior: Nearer to the head.<br>Example: The head is superior to the thorax.<br>---<br>Inferior: Nearer to the feet.<br>Example: The stomach is inferior to the heart.

Anterior (Ventral) / Posterior (Dorsal)

Anterior (Ventral): Nearer to the front.<br>Example: The quadriceps are anterior to the hamstrings.<br>---<br>Posterior (Dorsal): Nearer to the back.<br>Example: The hamstrings are posterior to the quadriceps.

Medial / Lateral

Medial: Nearer to the median plane.<br>Example: The nose is medial to the eyes.<br>---<br>Lateral: Farther from the median plane.<br>Example: The eyes are lateral to the nose.

Proximal / Distal

Proximal: Nearer to the trunk.<br>Example: The arms are proximal to the hands.<br>---<br>Distal: Farther from the trunk.<br>Example: The hands are distal to the arms.

Supine / Prone

Supine: Lying on the back, face up.<br>Example: A person performing a bench press is in a supine position.<br>---<br>Prone: Lying face down.<br>Example: A person performing a push-up is in a prone position.

Understanding these directional terms is essential for the next step: applying them to the body's planes of motion.

The Body Planes

Now that we have a standard starting point—the Anatomical Position—we can analyze movement by imagining the body is divided by imaginary flat surfaces called planes. These three primary planes are positioned at right angles to each other, creating a framework that helps us describe the path of motion for any given activity. All movements are described as occurring parallel to one of these planes.

Midsagittal (Median) Plane

This is a vertical plane that runs from front to back, dividing the body into right and left halves. While the midsagittal plane divides the body into two equal halves, any plane parallel to it is known as a sagittal plane. Movements that occur in this plane are forward and backward motions, such as walking, squatting, or cycling.

Frontal (Coronal) Plane

This is a vertical plane that runs from side to side, dividing the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) sections. Movements in this plane are lateral or side-to-side, such as doing jumping jacks or a side shuffle.

Transverse (Horizontal) Plane

This is a horizontal plane that divides the body into superior (upper) and inferior (lower) sections. Movements that occur parallel to the transverse plane are rotational, such as twisting the torso, swinging a golf club, or shaking your head "no."

These three planes not only describe motion but also intersect to define the body's central point.

Center of Gravity

The concept of the body planes leads us to another critical principle in kinesiology: the center of gravity. This is the strategic balance point of the body, around which mass is equally distributed. Understanding its location is essential for analyzing balance, stability, and how forces affect human movement.

The Center of Gravity is defined as the single point where the three primary body planes—median, frontal, and transverse—intersect. Conceptually, if you could support a person on a single point, this would be it; all of their weight would be perfectly balanced around it.

This point is crucial for understanding stability and how the body controls movement. Now that we understand the planes and the body's center, we can explore the specific movements that occur at the joints.

Joint Movements

All human motion occurs at joints, where two or more bones articulate. To describe these actions precisely, we use a specific set of anatomical terms. These movements are described as occurring in one of the three body planes we just discussed. They also typically occur in opposing pairs, where one action is the direct opposite of the other.

Paired Joint Movements Defined

  • Flexion: Reduces the angle between joints.
  • Extension: Increases the angle between joints.
  • Abduction: Movement away from the body's midline.
  • Adduction: Movement towards the midline.
  • Pronation: The palm faces posterior (backward).
  • Supination: The palm faces anterior (forward), as if holding a bowl of soup.
  • Dorsiflexion: The foot moves up toward the shin.
  • Plantar Flexion: The foot plants or points downward. Think of "planting" your foot into the ground to perform a toe raise.
  • Inversion: The sole of the foot moves in (medially).
  • Eversion: The sole of the foot moves out (laterally).
  • Medial Rotation: Also called internal rotation, this is movement around a bone's longitudinal axis that turns the anterior surface inward.
  • Lateral Rotation: Also called external rotation, this is movement around a bone's longitudinal axis that turns the anterior surface outward.

While these pairs describe most basic actions, we will now look at a special combination movement that uses several of these foundational actions.
